newsitem.title: FRANCE: INTERVIEW - Poor French air cargo trade outlook seen.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Poor French air cargo trade outlook seen.

text.p: The president of France's airfreight forwarding agents' association, SNAGFA, said that 1997 had so far been a disappointing year for the French air cargo industry.
Klaus Pfab told Reuters in an interview that, with the market still trying to break out of stagnation, the profitability outlook for companies operating in the sector remained bleak.
"The (French) air cargo cake is not growing and some of those wanting to ensure a slice of it will do so at any price," he said, in an oblique reference to cargo rate discounting.

He added: "Competition has grown fiercer and while most of this is coming from the integrators, they themselves are not totally free of problems. "UPS France is the prime example, with 1996 losses estimated by industry sources to total between 300 and 400 million francs," he said.

In the general interest of France's airfreight industry, one could expect more and more alliance-forging between the main protagonists -- airlines, agents and integrators -- without them necessarily being linked financially, he said.

"So far, 1997 has been below our expectations in volume terms and this is reflected in the moderate level rate increases implemented by several airlines in March and during the current month," Pfab pointed out.

"The traffic is just not there to justify significant rises. We are probably in for a new round of rate increases in the autumn but no-one would hazard a guess as to what degree -- any market forecasting is a perilous exercise these days," he said.
He thought that one positive factor was that airlines seemed to have finally understood the importance of giving prior notice to their cargo agents of rate increases.
"Maybe the difference of opinion we had with the airlines over the introduction of fuel surcharges had a salutary effect in this respect," Pfab said.
Although ex-Paris air cargo rates were relatively stable, observers said they were still relatively low.
Pfab felt airlines could be tempted to give priority to other higher yield generating European markets in preference to France.
In this case, French shippers and agents would find themselves confronted with a lack of capacity, he said.
He also pointed out that 1996 airport cargo traffic figures showed that London, Amsterdam and Frankfurt were achieving faster growth rates than Paris.
This was a "worrying trend", he noted.
